Hurricanes, floods, and earthquakes arrive with a visible point of impact. But many of today’s crises don’t. A conflict thousands of miles away can raise energy prices, disrupt food supplies, and strain budgets in countries on the other side of the world. As economic and climate shocks intensify and geopolitical tensions ripple across borders, governments need to be ready. 
To help countries prepare for these risks, the World Bank Group developed the Crisis Preparedness and Response Toolkit. Originally designed to strengthen preparedness for disasters and other emergencies, the Crisis Toolkit is now helping countries respond to a broader range of interconnected shocks, including those that spread through global energy, food, and economic systems. By combining pre-arranged financing, rapid-response mechanisms, and scalable support, it enables governments to access resources quickly, protect development gains, and strengthen resilience. Since its launch in 2024, 80 countries have adopted at least one of its instruments. 
Initially, countries mostly used the Crisis Toolkit’s instruments to prepare for and respond to disasters. When Hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica in 2025, the country was prepared and drew on multiple financing tools from the Crisis Toolkit put in place before the disaster. These included a pre-arranged credit line that can be drawn on quickly after a disaster or emergency, known as a Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option (Cat DDO), as well as financial protection through a catastrophe bond that pays out when pre-agreed conditions are met. The catastrophe bond provided a $150 million payout, while Jamaica also drew down the $42 million programmed under the Cat DDO as well as an additional $42 million in scalable financing that was available under the same facility. Together, these layers of financing gave Jamaica rapid access to resources, allowing the country to focus on response and recovery rather than scrambling to secure funds after the disaster struck.
In Colombia, following the recent earthquake, the government drew $200 million from a pre-arranged credit line through its Cat DDO. As needs became clearer, Colombia also accessed additional financing through the scalable option. These efforts reflect a broader shift toward embedding crisis preparedness and resilience into development planning, ensuring that countries are better positioned to withstand shocks when they occur. 
While natural disasters were the Crisis Toolkit’s first test, the ongoing Middle East conflict demonstrated something equally important: its ability to respond to crises without a clear geographic boundary. Unlike a localized natural disaster, its impacts have extended across borders, with countries far beyond the immediate conflict zone experiencing significant spillover effects. The crisis became the first large-scale demonstration of the Crisis Toolkit’s adaptability and scalability in responding to a complex, multi-country, and manmade shock. To date, 24 countries have received support for the Middle East conflict: 10 countries have reoriented financing toward crisis-related needs using the Crisis Toolkit, while 18 countries have accessed new financing, with some countries using both.
In Bangladesh, the government rapidly redirected funds from existing World Bank projects toward urgent needs through a Contingent Emergency Response Project (CERP). This type of project allows a country to repurpose and use part of the financing already available in its World Bank portfolio when a crisis creates new and immediate priorities. Faced with disruptions in global energy markets, Bangladesh redirected existing financing toward energy imports, helping mitigate nationwide power shortages and load-shedding.
In Djibouti, the government used a similar approach to address food insecurity, shortages of essential medicines, and wider economic spillovers associated with the crisis. By tapping into pre-approved financing, the government quickly channeled resources toward urgent priorities while helping protect vulnerable people from rising prices and constrained supplies.
In the Marshall Islands — a small island state far from the source of the conflict—the government used pre-arranged financing in existing World Bank projects to provide emergency top-up transfers for more than 41,000 people. It then complemented this with additional budget support through supplemental financing operation as needs evolved. Through the existing social protection system, the government reached households with support quickly, helping people cope with the rising costs and economic impacts associated with the fuel crisis.  
Preparedness is no longer just about responding to hurricanes, floods, or earthquakes. It is about helping countries navigate a world where risks are increasingly interconnected and where crises can emerge in unexpected ways. The Crisis Toolkit’s experience of the past two years shows that countries that invest in preparedness before a shock occurs are better positioned to protect people, safeguard development gains, and recover faster when crises hit.  As risks continue to evolve, the ability to adapt, respond at speed, and scale support when needed will be essential. The Crisis Preparedness and Response Toolkit is helping countries do exactly that.
